storyboard.title: The Conceptual Shift: Vectors as Data
The Rules of the Club: The 10 Axioms

section_1.title: Prerequisite: The Familiar Vector
section_1.content: Begin with the geometric intuition of vectors in R². Review how arrows can be added (head-to-tail) and scaled (stretched or shrunk). Establish that 'vector' usually brings to mind a physical direction and magnitude.
section_1.example: Visualizing a 'Navigation Drone' moving 3 units East and 4 units North. We represent this as a coordinate pair (3,4) and show the resulting arrow on a 2D grid.

section_2.title: The Conceptual Shift: Vectors as Data
section_2.content: Transition from geometry to abstraction. Explain that a 'vector' doesn't have to look like an arrow; it is simply an element of a set that obeys specific rules of addition and scaling. Introduce the idea of 'Information Containers'.
section_2.example: A 'Magic Potion Recipe' where 2 units of eye-of-newt and 3 units of dragon-scale represent a vector. Doubling the recipe (scaling) or adding it to another potion (addition) follows the same logic as arrows.

section_3.title: The Rules of the Club: The 10 Axioms
section_3.content: Introduce the formal definition of a Vector Space (V) over a field (F). Instead of listing all 10, focus on the 'Big Three' pillars: Closure (you don't leave the space), Existence of Zero (the 'nothing' element), and Additive Inverses (undoing an action). Use symbols paired with dynamic animations.
section_3.example: A 'Color Mixing App' where any color you mix remains a color (Closure), there is a 'transparent' paint (Zero), and for every color, there is a 'negative' that turns it back to transparent (Inverse).

section_4.title: Visualizing Function Spaces
section_4.content: Apply the abstract rules to functions—a concept usually seen as distinct from vectors. Show that if you add two functions, or multiply a function by a constant, you get another function. This introduces the 'Infinite Dimensional' concept visually.
section_4.example: Overlapping two sound waves (Sine waves) on an oscilloscope. The sum of the waves is a new wave, demonstrating that 'functions' inhabit a vector space just like arrows on a grid.

section_5.title: The Power of Abstraction
section_5.content: Summarize why we bother with abstraction. If we prove a theorem for a 'Vector Space,' it automatically applies to arrows, matrices, functions, and digital signals. It is the ultimate 'shortcut' in mathematics.
section_5.example: A 'Master Key' character that can unlock different doors labeled 'Quantum Mechanics', 'Computer Graphics', and 'Data Science' because they all speak the language of Vector Spaces.

lecture_lines: We often think of vectors as arrows in space.
Placing arrows head-to-tail shows vector addition in action.
Scaling an arrow changes its length but preserves direction.
A drone's path can be represented as a coordinate pair.
Together, these geometric properties define our intuitive vector.

Scaling an arrow changes its length but preserves direction.
A drone's path can be represented as a coordinate pair.
Together, these geometric properties define our intuitive vector.
Vectors are essentially containers for organized data.
A potion recipe represents a vector of ingredients.
Doubling the recipe is simply scaling the vector.

Formal vector spaces must satisfy ten specific axioms.
Closure means addition never leaves the set's boundaries.
The zero vector acts as the space's "nothing" element.
Inverses allow every action to be perfectly undone.
These rules allow for consistent mathematical behavior.
